The process parameters, which rely on laser stability and adequate energy density, are critical in achieving full density parts. The key parameters that contribute to the bulk properties of parts include laser hatch distance, laser speed, laser power, scanning strategy and rotation, beam offset, and spot size. These parameters work together to influence the thermal behavior of the melt pool, mechanical strength, surface roughness, and dimensional accuracy. If any inconsistencies are detected in density, mechanical behavior, or surface roughness during the AM process, additional builds, analysis, and machine adjustments should be performed until results are repeatable and reliable. 1.4 Acceptance Testing To ensure the quality of AM parts, it is essential to have a thorough understanding of the standard parts fabricated to meet specific needs. This knowledge is crucial for analyzing data during acceptance testing, as every aspect of the AM process, as summarized in Figure 10, plays a vital role in the final product's quality. Therefore, all these factors must be considered during acceptance testing, certification, and qualification. Moreover, in-situ monitoring and NDE should be performed to provide evidence of in-process and final quality, respectively. Many vendors have taken a proactive approach by incorporating quality assurance software and monitors in their machines, which enable real-time monitoring of key parameters such as laser power, melt pool behavior and solidification, thermal radiation, and void formation. While these tools are useful in predicting part quality, the lack of a standardized acceptance criterion necessitates the collection and archiving of all data, tests, measurements, and associated records to ensure the acceptance of AM parts. Completed Micro-Tensile Testing The micro-tension specimens, as shown in Figure 11, were subjected to rigorous testing on a Psylotech 10kN load frame to evaluate their mechanical properties. To ensure comprehensive analysis, specimens were fabricated in both horizontal and vertical orientations, with a minimum of five specimens tested for each condition. Digital image correlation was employed to accurately measure displacement, providing precise data for analysis. The compliance curves generated from these tests will demonstrate the repeatability of results in this setup. Notably, the orientation of the specimens was carefully controlled, with "H" specimens built horizontally but tested in the vertical (build direction) orientation, and "V" specimens built vertically but tested in the horizontal orientation. This deliberate approach ensures a thorough understanding of the specimens' behavior under different testing conditions. Figure 11: Micro-tension specimens. All dimensions are in mm.
